stimuli.title: Eight bank officers in a row, with departments
stimuli.content:
Eight officers of a bank, Anmol, Bishakha, Dolly, Gagandeep, Hrithik, Inaaya, Kirtan and Mehr, sit in a straight row, all facing north. Each works in a different department among Accounts, Audit, Credit, Forex, HR, IT, Legal and Treasury. (Facing north, a person's right is towards the east end of the row.)

- Inaaya sits fourth from the left end of the row and works in Credit.
- Bishakha sits second to the right of Inaaya and works in HR.
- The person who works in Accounts sits immediately to the right of Bishakha.
- Gagandeep sits at the extreme right end and works in Treasury.
- Dolly sits at an extreme end of the row, and Anmol sits immediately to the left of Inaaya.
- Mehr sits immediately to the left of Bishakha, and Kirtan is not an immediate neighbour of Bishakha.
- The person who works in IT sits second to the left of the person who works in Accounts.
- The person in Forex sits immediately to the right of the person in Legal, and Anmol does not work in Forex.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 8 from the left (west) end.
Step 1: Inaaya = 4 (Credit), Bishakha = 6 (HR), Accounts = 7, Gagandeep = 8 (Treasury).
Step 2: Dolly is at an end; seat 8 is taken, so Dolly = 1. Anmol = 3, Mehr = 5.
Step 3: Seats 2 and 7 remain for Hrithik and Kirtan. Kirtan cannot sit next to Bishakha (6), so Kirtan = 2 and Hrithik = 7 (Accounts).
Step 4: IT is two seats left of Accounts: seat 5, Mehr. Audit, Forex and Legal remain for seats 1, 2 and 3; Forex is immediately right of Legal, and Anmol (3) is not in Forex, so Legal = 1 (Dolly), Forex = 2 (Kirtan) and Audit = 3 (Anmol).

| Seat | Person | Department |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Dolly | Legal |
| 2 | Kirtan | Forex |
| 3 | Anmol | Audit |
| 4 | Inaaya | Credit |
| 5 | Mehr | IT |
| 6 | Bishakha | HR |
| 7 | Hrithik | Accounts |
| 8 | Gagandeep | Treasury |

stimuli.title: A row of unknown length and an interchange
stimuli.content:
Some persons sit in a straight row, all facing north. The number of persons in the row is not given. Harshit, Tejas, Vrinda and Yamuna are among them.

- Harshit sits tenth from the left end of the row, and Tejas sits somewhere to his right.
- If Harshit and Tejas interchange their seats, Harshit becomes seventeenth from the left end and Tejas becomes fourteenth from the right end.
- Vrinda sits exactly in the middle of the row.
- Yamuna sits second to the left of the seat that Tejas occupies before the interchange.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: After the interchange Harshit takes Tejas's seat and becomes 17th from the left, so Tejas sits 17th from the left.
Step 2: Tejas takes Harshit's seat (10th from the left) and becomes 14th from the right, so the row has 10 + 14 − 1 = 23 persons.
Step 3: Vrinda is in the middle: (23 + 1) ÷ 2 = 12th from the left. Yamuna is second to the left of 17th: 15th from the left.

| Person | From the left (before) | From the right (before) |
|---|---|---|
| Harshit | 10th | 14th |
| Vrinda | 12th | 12th |
| Yamuna | 15th | 9th |
| Tejas | 17th | 7th |

stimuli.title: Nine persons from three teams in one row
stimuli.content:
Nine persons Aaradhya, Bodhi, Chinmayi, Divit, Eshna, Falguni, Hridya, Ivaan and Jaanvi sit in a straight row, all facing north. Each belongs to one of three teams, Red, Blue and Green, and each team has exactly three members among them. (Facing north, the right is towards the east.)

- Jaanvi sits exactly in the middle of the row, and Falguni sits immediately to her left.
- Ivaan sits third to the right of Falguni, and they are in the same team.
- Divit sits at the extreme left end, and Eshna sits at the extreme right end.
- Aaradhya sits third to the left of Eshna, and Chinmayi sits immediately to the left of Eshna.
- Hridya sits to the left of Bodhi.
- No two members of the same team sit next to each other.
- Divit is in the Red team, and Aaradhya is in the Blue team.
- Jaanvi and Chinmayi are in the same team, and so are Hridya and Eshna.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 9 from the left end.
Step 1: Jaanvi = 5, Falguni = 4, Ivaan = 7, Divit = 1, Eshna = 9, Aaradhya = 6, Chinmayi = 8.
Step 2: Seats 2 and 3 remain for Hridya and Bodhi; Hridya is to the left: Hridya = 2, Bodhi = 3.
Step 3: Divit is Red and Aaradhya Blue. Jaanvi (5) and Ivaan (7) both sit next to Aaradhya, so neither is Blue, and so their team-mates Chinmayi and Falguni are not Blue either. Falguni sits next to Jaanvi, so the pair Falguni–Ivaan and the pair Jaanvi–Chinmayi take Red and Green in some order.
Step 4: If Falguni and Ivaan were Green, Jaanvi, Chinmayi and Divit would fill Red; Hridya and Eshna could not both join Green (it would have four), so they would be Blue and Bodhi Green — but Bodhi (3) sits next to Falguni (4) ✗. So Falguni and Ivaan are Red (Red is now full) and Jaanvi and Chinmayi are Green.
Step 5: Hridya and Eshna share a team; Red is full and Green has room for only one more, so both are Blue with Aaradhya, and Bodhi is the third Green member. No two neighbours share a team.

| Seat | Person | Team |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Divit | Red |
| 2 | Hridya | Blue |
| 3 | Bodhi | Green |
| 4 | Falguni | Red |
| 5 | Jaanvi | Green |
| 6 | Aaradhya | Blue |
| 7 | Ivaan | Red |
| 8 | Chinmayi | Green |
| 9 | Eshna | Blue |

stimuli.title: Seven persons around a round table, with favourite cuisines
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Ayaan, Gunika, Madhur, Parul, Rehaan, Sarika and Tanvir sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. Each likes a different cuisine among Bengali, Chinese, Gujarati, Italian, Mexican, Punjabi and Thai. (Facing the centre, a person's right is anticlockwise and the left is clockwise.)

- Parul sits immediately to the right of Ayaan, and Gunika sits third to the right of Ayaan.
- Madhur sits second to the left of Ayaan.
- Tanvir sits immediately between Parul and Gunika.
- Rehaan is an immediate neighbour of Ayaan.
- Ayaan likes Punjabi food, and the person who likes Thai food sits immediately to his right.
- Gunika likes Bengali food, and the person who likes Chinese food sits immediately to her right.
- The person who likes Mexican food sits immediately to the left of Ayaan.
- Madhur does not like Italian food.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 0 to 6 anticlockwise starting from Ayaan.
Step 1: Parul = 1 and Gunika = 3 (right = anticlockwise). Madhur is second to Ayaan's left (clockwise): 5.
Step 2: Tanvir sits between Parul (1) and Gunika (3): seat 2. Rehaan is next to Ayaan: seat 6 (seat 1 is Parul's). Sarika takes seat 4.
Step 3: Ayaan likes Punjabi; Thai is on his right: Parul. Gunika likes Bengali; Chinese is on her right: Sarika (4). Mexican is on Ayaan's left: Rehaan (6).
Step 4: Gujarati and Italian remain for Tanvir and Madhur; Madhur does not like Italian, so Madhur likes Gujarati and Tanvir Italian.

| Seat (anticlockwise) | Person | Cuisine |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Ayaan | Punjabi |
| 1 | Parul | Thai |
| 2 | Tanvir | Italian |
| 3 | Gunika | Bengali |
| 4 | Sarika | Chinese |
| 5 | Madhur | Gujarati |
| 6 | Rehaan | Mexican |

stimuli.title: Rectangular table: middle seats of the longer sides face outside
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Kshitij, Mahua, Nikunj, Prerak, Rumi, Sudhir, Tvisha and Urmila sit around a rectangular table. Three persons sit along each longer side and one person at each shorter side. The person in the middle seat of each longer side faces away from the centre; the other six face the centre. Each person on a longer side sits directly opposite a person on the other longer side. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; facing outside, it is clockwise.)

- Kshitij and Prerak sit at the two shorter sides of the table.
- Rumi sits immediately to the right of Kshitij.
- Mahua sits second to the right of Prerak.
- Urmila sits directly opposite Mahua.
- Nikunj sits immediately to the left of Urmila.
- Sudhir does not sit next to Prerak.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 0 to 7 anticlockwise, starting with Kshitij at one shorter side; Prerak is at the other shorter side, seat 4. Seats 1–3 and 5–7 are the longer sides (2 and 6 are their middle seats, facing outside), and seat s faces seat 8 − s.
Step 1: Kshitij faces the centre, so his right is anticlockwise: Rumi = 1.
Step 2: Prerak also faces the centre: Mahua = 4 + 2 = 6 (a middle seat, facing outside). Urmila is opposite Mahua: seat 2, also facing outside.
Step 3: Urmila faces outside, so her left is anticlockwise: Nikunj = 3.
Step 4: Seats 5 and 7 remain for Sudhir and Tvisha; seat 5 is next to Prerak, so Sudhir = 7, Tvisha = 5.

| Seat | Person | Position |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Kshitij | shorter side, facing the centre |
| 1 | Rumi | longer side, facing the centre |
| 2 | Urmila | middle of a longer side, facing outside |
| 3 | Nikunj | longer side, facing the centre |
| 4 | Prerak | shorter side, facing the centre |
| 5 | Tvisha | longer side, facing the centre |
| 6 | Mahua | middle of a longer side, facing outside |
| 7 | Sudhir | longer side, facing the centre |

stimuli.title: Three at an inner table, six at an outer table
stimuli.content:
Nine persons sit around two concentric circular tables. Three of them sit at the smaller inner table, equally spaced and facing outside; the other six sit at the outer table, equally spaced and facing the centre. Each person at the inner table directly faces one person at the outer table, and between any two such outer persons there is exactly one other outer person. The nine persons are Abeer, Deeksha, Faiyaz, Hamsini, Ishant, Kajol, Lakshit, Navin and Ojal. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; facing outside, it is clockwise.)

- Abeer, Kajol and Navin sit at the inner table; Abeer faces Hamsini.
- Kajol sits immediately to the left of Abeer.
- Faiyaz faces Kajol, and Deeksha sits immediately to the right of Faiyaz.
- Ishant sits immediately to the left of Hamsini.
- Lakshit sits second to the right of Faiyaz.
stimuli.solution:
Number the outer seats 0 to 5 anticlockwise from Hamsini, the person Abeer faces. The inner persons face outer seats 0, 2 and 4.
Step 1: Abeer faces outside, so his left is anticlockwise: Kajol is at the next inner seat anticlockwise and faces outer seat 2. Navin faces outer seat 4.
Step 2: Faiyaz faces Kajol: outer seat 2. Deeksha, to Faiyaz's right (anticlockwise): 3. Lakshit, second to Faiyaz's right: 4, so Lakshit faces Navin.
Step 3: Ishant is to Hamsini's left (clockwise): seat 5. Ojal takes seat 1.

| Outer seat | Outer person | Faced by (inner) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Hamsini | Abeer |
| 1 | Ojal | – |
| 2 | Faiyaz | Kajol |
| 3 | Deeksha | – |
| 4 | Lakshit | Navin |
| 5 | Ishant | – |

stimuli.title: Five floors and five vehicles
stimuli.content:
Five persons Amrit, Dimpy, Hari, Kanak and Sohan live on the five floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 5 the topmost). Each owns a different vehicle among a Bicycle, a Bike, a Car, a Scooter and a Van.

- Sohan lives exactly in the middle floor of the building and owns the Car.
- Amrit lives immediately above Sohan, and Kanak lives somewhere above Amrit.
- Dimpy lives on an even-numbered floor.
- The person who owns the Van lives on the lowermost floor.
- The person who owns the Scooter lives immediately above the person who owns the Bicycle.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Sohan = 3 (Car), Amrit = 4, Kanak = 5.
Step 2: Dimpy is on an even floor: 2 (floor 4 is Amrit's). Hari = 1, so Hari owns the Van.
Step 3: Bicycle, Bike and Scooter remain for floors 2, 4 and 5. The Scooter is immediately above the Bicycle: floors 4 and 5 (floor 3 is the Car). So Amrit has the Bicycle, Kanak the Scooter and Dimpy the Bike.

| Floor | Person | Vehicle |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Kanak | Scooter |
| 4 | Amrit | Bicycle |
| 3 | Sohan | Car |
| 2 | Dimpy | Bike |
| 1 | Hari | Van |

stimuli.title: Seven gift boxes in a stack
stimuli.content:
Seven boxes B, D, F, H, K, M and P are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom and 7 the top). Each box contains a different gift among a Clock, a Lamp, a Mug, a Pen set, a Scarf, a Toy and a Watch.

- Box P is kept exactly in the middle of the stack, and Box B is kept immediately below Box P.
- Only one box is kept between Box P and Box D, and Box D is kept above Box P.
- Box M is kept at the top of the stack.
- Box H contains the Watch, and it is kept immediately below Box D.
- Box F is kept below Box K, and Box B contains the Clock.
- The box containing the Toy is kept immediately above the box containing the Mug, and below the box containing the Watch.
- The box containing the Scarf is kept two places above the box containing the Lamp.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: P = 4, B = 3, D = 6, M = 7, H = 5 (Watch).
Step 2: Positions 1 and 2 remain for F and K; F is below K: F = 1, K = 2. B holds the Clock.
Step 3: Lamp, Mug, Pen set, Scarf and Toy remain for positions 1, 2, 4, 6 and 7. The Toy is immediately above the Mug and below the Watch (5): positions 1–2, so F has the Mug and K the Toy.
Step 4: The Scarf is two places above the Lamp: positions 4 and 6, so P has the Lamp, D the Scarf and M the Pen set.

| Position | Box | Gift |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | M | Pen set |
| 6 | D | Scarf |
| 5 | H | Watch |
| 4 | P | Lamp |
| 3 | B | Clock |
| 2 | K | Toy |
| 1 | F | Mug |

stimuli.title: Seven coloured boxes in a line on a shelf
stimuli.content:
Seven boxes Q, R, T, V, W, X and Y are placed side by side in a single line on a shelf. Left and right are as seen by a person facing the shelf. Each box is of a different colour among Beige, Blue, Grey, Lemon, Olive, Peach and Teal.

- Box T is placed exactly in the middle of the line, and Box R is placed immediately to the right of Box T.
- Box Q is placed second to the left of Box T, and Box Y is placed immediately to the right of Box Q.
- Box W is placed at the extreme left end, and Box V at the extreme right end.
- Box T is Blue, and the Peach box is placed immediately to the left of the Blue box.
- The Teal box is at the left end and the Beige box at the right end.
- The Grey box is placed between the Teal box and the Peach box.
- The Olive box is placed immediately to the right of the Blue box.
stimuli.solution:
Number the places 1 to 7 from the left.
Step 1: T = 4, R = 5, Q = 2, Y = 3, W = 1, V = 7, so X = 6.
Step 2: T is Blue; Peach is immediately left of it: Y. Teal = 1 (W), Beige = 7 (V).
Step 3: Grey lies between Teal (1) and Peach (3): place 2, Q. Olive is immediately right of Blue: R. Lemon is left for X.

|---|---|---|

| 2 | Q | Grey |
| 3 | Y | Peach |
| 4 | T | Blue |
| 5 | R | Olive |

stimuli.title: Nine boxes in three stacks of different heights
stimuli.content:
Nine boxes B, C, F, J, L, N, R, U and Z are kept in three stacks standing side by side: the Left stack has two boxes, the Middle stack three and the Right stack four. Level 1 is the bottom of every stack; 'directly above/below' means in the same stack, one level higher/lower.

- Box L is at the top of the tallest stack, and Box R is directly below Box L.
- Box U is directly below Box R. Box B is in the middle stack, at the same level as Box U.
- Box N is directly above Box B.
- Box C is at the top of a stack, and Box J is directly below Box C.
- Box Z is not in the same stack as Box L.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: The tallest stack is the Right one: L = Right 4, R = Right 3, U = Right 2.
Step 2: B is in the Middle stack at U's level: Middle 2. N is directly above B: Middle 3, the top of that stack.
Step 3: C is at the top of a stack with J directly below it. Right and Middle tops are taken, so C = Left 2 and J = Left 1.
Step 4: Middle 1 and Right 1 remain for F and Z. Z is not in L's (Right) stack: Z = Middle 1, F = Right 1.

| Level | Left | Middle | Right |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | – | – | L |
| 3 | – | N | R |
| 2 | C | B | U |
| 1 | J | Z | F |

stimuli.title: Two stacks, lighter boxes always on top
stimuli.content:
Eight boxes D, E, G, H, K, M, P and T are kept in two stacks, A and B, with four boxes in each stack (level 1 is the bottom of a stack). Their weights are 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24 kg, one weight per box. In each stack, every box is lighter than the box directly below it.

- Box T is the heaviest box and is in stack A.
- Box K is at the top of stack B and weighs 7 kg.
- Box M is the lightest box.
- Box H is at the bottom of stack B and weighs 3 kg less than Box T.
- Box G is kept directly below Box D.
- Box P weighs twice as much as Box E.
- Box G is in the same stack as Box T.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Every stack gets lighter upwards, so the heaviest box is at the bottom of its stack: T = A1 (24 kg). K = B4 (7 kg). H = B1 with 24 − 3 = 21 kg.
Step 2: The lightest box M (5 kg) must be at the top of a stack; B4 is K, so M = A4.
Step 3: D, E, G and P take A2, A3, B2 and B3 with 9, 12, 15 and 18 kg. P = 2 × E, so P = 18 and E = 9; G and D share 12 and 15.
Step 4: G is directly below D and in T's stack, so G and D are in stack A (G = A2, D = A3) and P, E are in stack B. In each stack the lower box is heavier: G = 15, D = 12, P = B2 (18), E = B3 (9).

| Level | Stack A | Stack B |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | M (5 kg) | K (7 kg) |
| 3 | D (12 kg) | E (9 kg) |
| 2 | G (15 kg) | P (18 kg) |
| 1 | T (24 kg) | H (21 kg) |

stimuli.title: Five colour words for comparisons
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, colour words are used between two letters with these meanings:
'A pink B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A blue B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A red B' means 'A is either greater than or equal to B'; 'A grey B' means 'A is either smaller than or equal to B'; 'A green B' means 'A is equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: pink means >, blue means <, red means ≥, grey means ≤ and green means =. Rewrite every statement with ordinary signs, join them into one chain and test each conclusion along it.

stimuli.title: Six exams on the weekdays of March 2027
stimuli.content:
Six exams — Chemistry, Hindi, Physics, Sanskrit, Statistics and Zoology — are held on six different dates in March 2027, one exam per date. No exam is held on a Saturday or a Sunday. 1 March 2027 is a Monday.

- The Statistics exam is on the first Wednesday of the month.
- The Physics exam is exactly 15 days after the Statistics exam.
- The Hindi exam is on the last Friday of the month.
- The Chemistry exam is on the same day of the week as the Physics exam, exactly one week earlier.
- The Zoology exam is on the first Monday after the Chemistry exam.
- The Sanskrit exam is on a date that is a multiple of 10, before the Hindi exam.
stimuli.solution:
Mondays of March 2027: 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, so Wednesdays are 3, 10, 17, 24, 31 and Fridays 5, 12, 19, 26. Statistics: first Wednesday, 3rd. Physics: 3 + 15 = 18th (Thursday). Hindi: last Friday, 26th. Chemistry: 18 − 7 = 11th (Thursday). Zoology: first Monday after the 11th, the 15th. Sanskrit: multiples of 10 are 10 (Wednesday), 20 (Saturday, no exams) and 30 (after Hindi), so the 10th.

Order: Statistics 3 (Wed), Sanskrit 10 (Wed), Chemistry 11 (Thu), Zoology 15 (Mon), Physics 18 (Thu), Hindi 26 (Fri).

stimuli.title: Seven book launches from April to October, in three genres
stimuli.content:
Seven authors Amit, Bhanu, Charu, Dhruva, Esha, Firdaus and Gunjan each launch one book in a different month from April to October of the same year. Each book belongs to one of three genres: Poetry, Fiction or Travel.

- No two books launched in consecutive months are of the same genre.
- Three of the books are Poetry, two are Fiction and two are Travel.
- Charu's book, a Poetry book, is launched in July.
- Esha's book is launched in the month immediately before Charu's, and it is not a Fiction book.
- Amit's book is launched in the first of the seven months and Gunjan's in the last, and neither of their books is Poetry.
- Firdaus's book is a Fiction book launched in a month that has 31 days.
- The two Fiction books are launched exactly four months apart.
- Bhanu's book is launched later than Dhruva's.
stimuli.solution:
Charu: July, Poetry. Esha: June; her book is not Fiction, and it cannot be Poetry next to Charu's Poetry July, so it is Travel. Amit: April, Gunjan: October, neither Poetry. Two more Poetry books are needed among May, August and September (April and October are not Poetry); August touches Charu's Poetry July, so May and September are Poetry. Firdaus (Fiction, 31-day month: May or August) therefore takes August, and Dhruva and Bhanu take May and September — Bhanu later, so Dhruva May, Bhanu September. The second Fiction book must be four months from August: April (Amit), since October is only two months away. Gunjan's book is then Travel.

Apr Amit (Fiction), May Dhruva (Poetry), Jun Esha (Travel), Jul Charu (Poetry), Aug Firdaus (Fiction), Sep Bhanu (Poetry), Oct Gunjan (Travel).

stimuli.title: Six bank branches and their opening years
stimuli.content:
A bank opened six branches — Alwar, Bidar, Churu, Dhule, Etah and Gonda — in six different years. The age of a branch in a year is the number of years completed since it opened (a branch opened in 2006 is 20 years old in 2026).

- In 2026, the Churu branch completes exactly 20 years.
- In 2026, the Alwar branch is exactly twice as old as the Churu branch.
- The Gonda branch opened seven years after the Churu branch.
- The Etah branch opened in a leap year, after the Churu branch but before the Gonda branch, and its age in 2026 is a multiple of 7.
- In 2026, the age of the Dhule branch equals the sum of the ages of the Gonda and Etah branches.
- The Bidar branch opened in the year in which the Alwar branch completed 10 years.
stimuli.solution:
Churu: 2026 − 20 = 2006. Alwar: 40 years old, 1986. Gonda: 2013. Etah: a leap year after 2006 and before 2013 is 2008 or 2012; ages 18 and 14, and only 14 is a multiple of 7: 2012. Dhule: 13 + 14 = 27 years, 1999. Bidar: Alwar completed 10 years in 1996.

Oldest to newest: Alwar 1986, Bidar 1996, Dhule 1999, Churu 2006, Etah 2012, Gonda 2013.

stimuli.title: Seven points with diagonal steps
stimuli.content:
Seven points P, Q, R, S, T, U and V lie on flat ground.

stimuli.title: Three rows of numbers with square and prime rules
stimuli.content:
Each row has three numbers. Work from left to right: apply the first rule below that fits the first two numbers, then apply the first rule that fits that result and the third number. The final value is the row's result.

(i) If the first number of the pair is a perfect square, the result is its square root multiplied by the second number.
(ii) Otherwise, if the first number is a prime number, the result is the first number plus twice the second number.
(iii) Otherwise, if the second number is even it is subtracted from the first; if it is odd it is added to the first.

Row 1: 16   5   3
Row 2: 7   6   4
Row 3: 25   3   9
stimuli.solution:
Row 1: 16 is a square → 4 × 5 = 20; 20 is neither a square nor a prime and 3 is odd → 23.
Row 2: 7 is prime → 7 + 12 = 19; 19 is prime → 19 + 8 = 27.
Row 3: 25 is a square → 5 × 3 = 15; 15 is neither, 9 is odd → 24.

stimuli.title: Machine: odd numbers first
stimuli.content:
A number arrangement machine rearranges a line of numbers step by step. In each step it takes, among the numbers not yet arranged, the smallest odd number and places it immediately to the right of the numbers already arranged at the left end (in Step I, at the extreme left). When no odd number is left, it takes the smallest even number in the same way. The other numbers keep their order. A step that would not change the line is not counted, and the machine stops when the arrangement is complete.

Input: 42 17 68 33 91 24 55

stimuli.title: Machine: word-number pairs to the right
stimuli.content:
A word and number arrangement machine rearranges a line step by step. In each step it takes the word that comes first in alphabetical order among the words not yet arranged and the smallest number among the numbers not yet arranged. It adds the number of letters in that word to that number, and places the word followed by the new number at the right end, immediately to the left of the pairs already placed there (in Step I, at the extreme right). All other elements keep their order. The machine stops when every element has been arranged.

Input: violet 28 amber 73 coral 46 indigo 15 olive 59
stimuli.solution:
Pairs in order: amber + 15 → 20, coral + 28 → 33, indigo + 46 → 52, olive + 59 → 64, violet + 73 → 79.

Step I: violet 28 73 coral 46 indigo olive 59 amber 20
Step II: violet 73 46 indigo olive 59 coral 33 amber 20
Step III: violet 73 olive 59 indigo 52 coral 33 amber 20
Step IV: violet 73 olive 64 indigo 52 coral 33 amber 20
Step V: violet 79 olive 64 indigo 52 coral 33 amber 20

stimuli.title: Machine: middle digits and swapped ends
stimuli.content:
A number arrangement machine rearranges a line of three-digit numbers step by step. In each step it takes, among the numbers not yet arranged, the one with the smallest middle (tens) digit, interchanges its first and last digits, and places the new number immediately to the right of the numbers already arranged at the left end (in Step I, at the extreme left). The other numbers keep their order. The machine stops when every number has been arranged.

- Exactly two floors lie between the two members of each family.
- Charu lives on the topmost floor, and Bela on the lowermost floor.
- Uma lives immediately above Anil.

Who lives on floor 2?

solution.concept: A fixed gap between family members pairs the floors
solution.explanation: With two floors between family members, the family pairs must occupy floors 1–4, 2–5 and 3–6. Charu is on 6, so Dev is on 3. Bela is on 1, so Anil is on 4. Uma is immediately above Anil: floor 5, so Vikas is on floor 2.
solution.why_others_wrong: Dev lives on floor 3, Anil on 4 and Uma on 5.

A building has seven floors, numbered 1 (lowermost) to 7 (topmost). Five persons Gul, Jas, Ketki, Lalan and Mona live in it, one person per floor, so two floors are vacant.
- Jas lives on the topmost floor, and Lalan lives immediately below Jas.
- Exactly two floors lie between Jas and Gul.
- Mona lives immediately below Gul.
- Ketki lives on an odd-numbered floor.
- The two vacant floors are not next to each other.

How many vacant floors are there below Gul?

solution.concept: Place the persons, then read the gaps
solution.explanation: Jas = 7, Lalan = 6, Gul = 4, Mona = 3. Floors 1, 2 and 5 remain for Ketki and the two vacant floors. Ketki is on an odd floor (1 or 5); if Ketki were on 5, floors 1 and 2 would both be vacant and next to each other. So Ketki = 1 and floors 2 and 5 are vacant. One vacant floor (2) is below Gul.

- Ojaswini lives on floor 3, and Rekha lives immediately above her.
- Exactly three floors lie between Ojaswini and Prithu, and Prithu lives above her.
- Quresh lives on the topmost floor, and the number of floors above Prithu equals the number of floors below Ojaswini.
- Sunil lives immediately below Quresh, and Tanu lives on the lowermost floor.

How many vacant floors lie between Rekha and Prithu?

solution.concept: Find the height of the building from the 'equal number of floors' clue
solution.explanation: Ojaswini = 3, Rekha = 4, Prithu = 3 + 4 = 7. Two floors lie below Ojaswini, so two lie above Prithu: the building has 9 floors and Quresh = 9, Sunil = 8, Tanu = 1. The vacant floors are 2, 5 and 6, and two of them (5 and 6) lie between Rekha (4) and Prithu (7).
steps: Floors below Ojaswini = 2 ⇒ floors above Prithu = 2 ⇒ 9 floors

Nine persons Arpita, Bhaskar, Damini, Eshaan, Gopika, Indu, Jayesh, Meghna and Pranav live in the building, one per flat, so three flats are vacant.
- Arpita lives in the North flat of floor 4, and Pranav lives in the other flat on her floor.
- Indu lives directly above Pranav, and Gopika lives directly below Arpita.
- Jayesh lives in a North flat on the topmost floor; the other flat on his floor and the flat directly below his are both vacant.
- Eshaan lives in the South flat of the lowermost floor, and Bhaskar lives directly above Eshaan.
- Damini lives directly below Meghna.

How many persons live in South flats?

solution.concept: Track the vacant flats as carefully as the occupied ones
solution.explanation: Arpita = 4 North, Pranav = 4 South, Indu = 5 South, Gopika = 3 North. Jayesh = 6 North, with 6 South and 5 North vacant. Eshaan = 1 South, Bhaskar = 2 South. Free flats: 1 North, 2 North and 3 South; Damini is directly below Meghna, which only 1 North / 2 North allow, so 3 South is the third vacant flat. South-flat residents: Eshaan, Bhaskar, Pranav and Indu — four.
steps: Damini below Meghna ⇒ 1N Damini, 2N Meghna; 3S vacant

Statements:
All sardines are prawns.
Some lobsters are sardines.

Conclusions:
I. Some lobsters are prawns.
II. All prawns are sardines.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Two-statement syllogism (Venn diagram method)
solution.explanation: The lobsters that are sardines are inside the prawns, so some lobsters are prawns (I). 'All sardines are prawns' cannot be reversed into 'All prawns are sardines' (II).
steps: Lobster ∩ sardine ≠ ∅ and sardines ⊂ prawns ⇒ some lobsters are prawns: I follows
All A are B does not give All B are A ⇒ II not certain
solution.why_others_wrong: Conclusion II is not forced by the statements (some valid diagram breaks it), so 'Both' and 'Only II' are wrong; I holds in every diagram, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

Only statements II and III together are sufficient
Even all three statements together are not sufficient
All three statements I, II and III together are necessary

Any pair leaves A or D unconnected

Only statements I and III together are sufficient

Even all three statements together are not sufficient

All three statements I, II and III together are necessary
Even all three statements together are not sufficient

I + II and I + III leave Arun open

Both I and II are implicit

Most of the bank's rural customers do not use the internet, and very few of them took part in the online poll

solution.concept: Weaken: show that the sample does not represent the people affected
solution.explanation: The decision affects rural customers, but the poll mostly reached internet users. If rural customers hardly took part and mostly do not use the internet, the poll says nothing about their needs.
steps: Weakener: they were missing from the poll
solution.why_others_wrong: A large number of responses does not fix a biased sample; branch costs and city customers' habits do not show how rural customers would be affected.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Most of the bank's rural customers do not use the internet, and very few of them took part in the online poll

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: The city should set up more public charging points for electric cars, because the lack of charging points is what is holding back the purchase of electric cars in the city.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.text: Electric cars are cheaper to run than petrol cars
The city has more than five lakh registered cars
Charging points can be installed in parking lots
In a survey, most car buyers in the city who had considered an electric car said they did not buy one because they had nowhere to charge it

solution.concept: Strengthen: confirm the cause the argument names
solution.explanation: The argument says the shortage of charging points is the obstacle. The survey shows that buyers who considered electric cars were put off for exactly that reason.
steps: Claim: lack of charging points blocks purchases
Strengthener: buyers say so in a survey
solution.why_others_wrong: Running costs and the number of cars do not show what stops buyers; that charging points can be installed shows the plan is possible, not that it would help.
solution.final_answer: Option D: In a survey, most car buyers in the city who had considered an electric car said they did not buy one because they had nowhere to charge it

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: A theatre sells balcony tickets at ₹300 each and stall tickets at ₹200 each. On Saturday it sold 150 tickets in all and collected ₹38,000 from them.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.text: The theatre sold 80 balcony tickets on Saturday
The theatre sold 70 balcony tickets on Saturday
The theatre sold more stall tickets than balcony tickets on Saturday
The theatre collected ₹16,000 from stall tickets on Saturday

solution.concept: Two conditions fix two unknowns
solution.explanation: If b balcony tickets were sold, 300b + 200(150 − b) = 38,000, so 100b = 8,000 and b = 80. Then 70 stall tickets were sold, bringing in ₹14,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: 70 is the number of stall tickets; stall tickets (70) were fewer than balcony tickets (80); stall income was ₹14,000, not ₹16,000.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The theatre sold 80 balcony tickets on Saturday

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: After a new highway opened near a district hospital, the number of patients in its emergency ward has doubled, and many of them wait for hours before a doctor sees them.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Add doctors and beds to the emergency ward and set up a trauma-care unit to treat highway accident cases
Refuse to treat patients from other districts
Reduce the working hours of the emergency ward

solution.concept: Match capacity to the new demand
solution.explanation: Demand has doubled, mainly from the highway. More doctors and beds, plus a trauma unit, add the capacity the ward now needs.
steps: Remedy: more staff, beds and a trauma unit
solution.why_others_wrong: Closing the highway is impractical; refusing patients and cutting hours make the problem worse.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Add doctors and beds to the emergency ward and set up a trauma-care unit to treat highway accident cases

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Shops on Gandhi Road that put up bright LED signboards last year reported higher sales this year than the shops on the road that did not. So bright signboards increase a shop's sales.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: LED signboards use less electricity than older signboards
The shops that put up LED signboards were the same shops that also enlarged their premises and stocked more goods last year
Some shops on Gandhi Road stay open until 10 pm
Gandhi Road is one of the busiest roads in the town

solution.concept: Weaken: point to another difference between the two groups
solution.explanation: If the shops with new signboards also expanded and added stock, their higher sales could come from the expansion, not the signboards.
steps: Weakener: those shops also expanded ⇒ another cause
solution.why_others_wrong: Electricity use, opening hours of some shops and the road's traffic apply to both groups and do not explain the difference.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The shops that put up LED signboards were the same shops that also enlarged their premises and stocked more goods last year

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: In a quiz tournament, each of five teams played every other team exactly once. Each match had a winner and a loser; the winner got 2 points and the loser 0.

Which of the following must be true?

options.text: Each team won exactly two matches
At least one team won all its matches
The five teams together got 20 points
The five teams together got 10 points

solution.concept: Count matches first
solution.explanation: Five teams playing each other once make 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 matches, and each match gives out exactly 2 points, so the teams together got 20 points.
solution.why_others_wrong: The results of individual teams are not given, so 'two wins each' and 'one unbeaten team' need not be true; 10 is the number of matches, not points.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The five teams together got 20 points

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: The city's decision to make the first hour of parking free in the old market area will bring more shoppers to the old market.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.text: The old market has more than 200 shops
Parking charges in the city were last revised five years ago
Some shoppers in the old market come on foot
Shopkeepers in the old market say that many of their former customers now shop at the new mall mainly because parking there is free

solution.concept: Strengthen: show that parking cost is what keeps shoppers away
solution.explanation: If shoppers left the old market mainly because they had to pay for parking, free parking removes that reason and is likely to bring some of them back.
steps: Strengthener: paid parking is why shoppers left
solution.why_others_wrong: The number of shops and when charges were last revised do not link parking to shoppers; shoppers on foot are unaffected by parking.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Shopkeepers in the old market say that many of their former customers now shop at the new mall mainly because parking there is free

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: A bank has found that many people who took small business loans under a government scheme did not know that the loans had to be repaid, and defaults on these loans are rising.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Explain the repayment terms clearly to every borrower when the loan is given, and send reminders before each instalment falls due
Stop giving loans under the scheme
Write off all the loans given under the scheme
Take legal action against every borrower at once

solution.concept: Remove the misunderstanding that causes the problem
solution.explanation: Defaults are rising because borrowers did not know they had to repay. Clear explanation at the start and reminders later remove that gap without ending the scheme.
solution.why_others_wrong: Stopping the scheme or writing off loans is extreme; suing every borrower punishes people for a misunderstanding that the bank can correct.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Explain the repayment terms clearly to every borrower when the loan is given, and send reminders before each instalment falls due

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Since the city introduced a ₹2,000 fine for driving without a seat belt, the number of drivers caught without a seat belt has fallen by 60%. So many more drivers in the city now wear seat belts.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: The fine for not wearing a helmet was also raised during the same period
During the same period, the traffic police cut the number of seat-belt checkpoints in the city by about two-thirds
Most new cars warn drivers who have not fastened their seat belts
Many drivers support the higher fine

solution.concept: Weaken: show that the measure itself changed
solution.explanation: The number of drivers caught depends on how many checks are made. If checkpoints fell by two-thirds, far fewer drivers would be caught even if just as many drove without seat belts.
steps: Weakener: far fewer checks ⇒ catches no longer measure behaviour
solution.why_others_wrong: The helmet fine concerns two-wheelers; seat-belt warnings in new cars would, if anything, support the argument; drivers' support for the fine does not show what they do.
solution.final_answer: Option B: During the same period, the traffic police cut the number of seat-belt checkpoints in the city by about two-thirds
